title: Exhibition at Leopold Museum pairs works by Herbert Boeckl and Hans Josephsohn
summary: Select paintings by the eminent Austrian painter Herbert Boeckl (1894–1966) enter into a tension-filled dialogue with sculptures by the Swiss sculptor Hans Josephsohn (1920–2012) in the exhibition Herbert Boeckl – Hans Josephsohn. Figural Archetypes which addresses existential and universal questions of humanity, and will open up new spaces of association. Though the two artists never met, their oeuvres show fundamental parallels in terms of their form-finding processes and their concepts of corporeality and materiality. Irrespective of their differences with regards to historical, geographical and cultural constructs, the juxtaposition reveals surprising analogies in their works regarding formal esthetics and phenomenology. title: The first family of the Marvel age: The ultimate collection of the world's greatest comic magazine
summary: Hoping to break out of a sales slump at Marvel in the early 1960s, veteran comic creators Stan Lee and Jack Kirby hit on the idea of doing a super-team. Kirby, who thought super heroes were due for a revival after 15 years of being pushed aside by romance, horror, and war comics, saw it as smart business. Lee just once wanted to “do the type of story I myself would enjoy reading.” The Fantastic Four forever changed their careers, their lives, and the comic book industry. Some of the most iconic moments in Marvel history are here, starting with Reed Richards, his girlfriend Sue Storm, his best friend Ben Grimm, and her little brother Johnny Storm crash landing their rocket after it has been hit by cosmic rays and discovering they have been transformed into Mr. Fantastic, the Invisible Girl, the Thing, and the Human Torch in issue No. 1. title: Georgia Museum of Art releases expanded second edition of Richard Hunt catalogue
summary: Over his seven-decade career, Chicago native Richard Hunt (1935 – 2023) became one of the nation’s most prolific public sculptors, creating 160 large-scale commissions in 24 different states and Washington, D.C. Made of welded and cast steel, aluminum, copper and bronze, his abstract creations often resemble natural forms, whether plant or animal. Often seen as a post-Black artist, Hunt in fact promotes ideals of freedom and equality through his work. His career spanned the length of the Civil Rights and Black Power movements into modern-day campaigns for social justice, and many of his monuments commemorate historic figures such as Emmett Till, Ida B. Wells and Martin Luther King, Jr. Bridging the gap between abstract art and the Black experience, he intertwines inspiration from his ancestry and identity with that from history, mythology and spirituality. title: Tate Modern opens first major UK exhibition of Ana Mendieta in over a decade
summary: Tate Modern presents the UK’s first major exhibition dedicated to multidisciplinary artist Ana Mendieta (1948-1985) in over a decade. Active in the 1970s and 1980s, Mendieta’s ground-breaking practice challenged traditional notions of sculpture, photography and film. Using her own terms to describe her art, she is best known for her ‘earth-body’ works, outlining her body in the landscape with natural elements such as earth, fire and flowers. Featuring over 120 works, the exhibition is arranged thematically through symbolic locations, highlighting key moments in the artist’s career and demonstrating her persistent engagement with the natural world. Her iconic Silueta Series 1973-80 is presented alongside newly remastered films, rarely seen paintings and drawings, late sculptures and restaged installations, shedding new light on her practice and demonstrating its lasting power for new audiences. title: LE BAL presents photography collection of Michael and Jane Wilson
summary: To mark the bicentenary of the birth of photography, LE BAL is presenting, for the first time, an exhibition devoted to a single collection: that of Michael and Jane Wilson / The Wilson Centre for Photography. Through this rare ensemble of 120 prints, the exhibition explores the sometimes elusive, sometimes luminous, always shifting relationship between the one who photographs and the one who is photographed. From fleeting encounters to carefully staged collaborations, from images caught in the moment to collaboratively constructed scenes, the exhibition examines the relationship that comes into being, at the moment the photograph is made, between the photographer and their subject. What does the image reveal about the respective positions of these two bodies? title: Artist Yu Nishimura explores themes of displacement in exhibition at Sadie Coles HQ
summary: Throughout the development of Dislocation, Yu Nishimura articulated an approach to painting grounded in temporal, spatial, and psychological displacement. Across the exhibition, images emerge through layers of revision, interruption, and residual marks, producing compositions that resist fixed resolution and instead remain suspended between memory, perception and reconstruction. Place and landscape are strongly present, yet rather than depicting specific locations, the paintings allow the gaze and the body to enter the landscape itself — moving closer to the subject and then withdrawing again, gradually shaping a felt sense of space. This shifting proximity produces a quiet recalibration of the viewer’s position where distance is never stable but continuously negotiated. Figures, landscapes, objects and architectural details appear partially detached, occupying uncertain spaces

title: Sally Mann survey traces five decades of photography in Macula et Materia
summary: Sally Mann (born in Lexington, Virginia, 1951) is one of the most important figures in contemporary American photography. Active since the late sixties, she has built up a consistent and demanding body of work that primarily focuses on her native region of the American South, which she continues to explore. She has received many awards, including grants from the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Endowment for the Humanities and the Guggenheim Foundation, and her work is now held in the collections of major international institutions. From the outset, Sally Mann has been part of a photographic tradition that pays attention to the materiality of the medium and its place in history. Self-taught, she developed an early practice based on the use of large-format cameras, which demand patience, precision and technical rigour. title: Bienvenu Steinberg & C presents group exhibition 'Between the Lines'
summary: Bienvenu Steinberg & C is presenting Between the Lines, an exhibition featuring Johanna Calle, Jonathan Callan, Stefana McClure, Glenda León, Ivan Lam, Sean Micka, Nobuhira Narumi, Ed Ruscha, Analia Saban, and Adam Winner on view through August 29, 2026. Between the Lines is an exhibition with no underlining—it hints, suggests, and infers. The ten included artists playfully dig into an unparalleled present, relieving us through their archaeological gestures. A summer outing that could leave you ice cold. Johanna Calle (b. 1965) lives and works in Bogotá, Colombia. Her work draws on a range of archival and deciphering techniques, often associated with everyday life, to address the violence of recent Colombian history. title: Rashid Johnson organizes sweeping summer exhibition at Hauser & Wirth Menorca
summary: On view this summer at Hauser & Wirth Menorca, Directionless is a sweeping group exhibition organized by Rashid Johnson, who has invited Charles Gaines, Firelei Báez and Cristina Iglesias to nominate artists from beyond the gallery’s roster. The most extensive exhibition staged in Menorca to date, it takes over all the galleries and outdoor landscape of Illa del Rei, featuring 28 artists from more than 10 countries. The artist-driven project begins from the premise that we are living in a moment of profound disorientation. Rather than offering resolution, the exhibition asks how artists might productively inhabit this uncertainty—how they develop new vocabularies and provisional orientations when established coordinates begin to fail. “We are all living inside a shared sense of disorientation right now—one that is evolving with increasing momentum.

title: Berlin exhibition imagines the rituals of eating and drinking in 2101
summary: What might dinner look like 75 years from now? Will people still gather around a shared table, prepare tea together or pass food from one person to another? Or will climate disruption, crowded megacities and increasingly digital lives transform even the most familiar rituals of eating and drinking? A new exhibition now on view at Berlin’s Kunstgewerbemuseum invites visitors to consider those questions through experimental porcelain, speculative design and imagined social customs. Titled “2101 – Future Ceramics. Table Culture of the Future,” the exhibition brings together 12 projects created by product design students at the Berlin University of the Arts. It is on view through February 28, 2027. The project began with a deceptively simple question: How will people live in the year 2101? title: Pace announces details for its September exhibition program across its New York and Los Angeles galleries
summary: Pace will present KNOTTING, TYING, FOLDING, an exhibition of sculptures by Lynda Benglis, at its 540 West 25th Street gallery from September 11 through October 24. Alongside glazed ceramic, bronze, pleated, and paper works created by Benglis between 1972 and 2024, the presentation will also spotlight rarely exhibited glass sculptures from 1985. This presentation follows the recent exhibition Encounters: Giacometti x Lynda Benglis at the Barbican Centre in London—organized as part of a series pairing contemporary artists’ work with Alberto Giacometti’s sculptures. Next year, Benglis will be the subject of a major retrospective at Kunstmuseum Basel (March 13 – August 1, 2027), which will then travel to Tate Modern (September 30, 2027 – March 5, 2028) and Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Denmark (dates to be announced), as well as a solo presentation, Lynda Benglis: Elemental, at the Newcomb Art Museum of Tulane University (January 20 – May 20, 2027), which wi

title: Brancusi: Already the most successful exhibition since 2012
summary: With more than 300,000 visitors expected by the close of its run on 9 August, the special exhibition Brancusi is set to become the most visited exhibition at the Neue Nationalgalerie since Gerhard Richter in 2012. The ten visitors who bring the exhibition's total attendance to 300,000 will each receive an exhibition catalogue. In response to the sustained high level of public interest, the museum is extending its opening hours for the exhibition's final weekend on 7 and 8 August and offering additional personal tours with the curators and the director. Since opening on 20 March 2026, this unique collaboration with the Centre Pompidou in Paris has brought together more than 150 works by the Romanian-French sculptor and marks the first comprehensive retrospective of Constantin Brancusi's work in Germany in more than 50 years. title: Pace Gallery brings together 27 artists for summer show in Berlin
summary: Pace is presenting Goodbye Sadness, Hello Sadness, a group exhibition of paintings, sculptures, and photographs by an international group of twenty-seven artists, at its Berlin gallery from July 4 through August 23. Goodbye Sadness, Hello Sadness takes its title from Bonjour Tristesse, the 1954 novel written by the then 18-year-old Françoise Sagan. The book’s hedonistic, carefree spirit—ultimately giving way to a disquieting loss of innocence—infuses the exhibition in Berlin, which coalesces around the nighttime as a setting for possibility and ambiguity. The same phrase in two parts—Goodbye Sadness and Hello Sadness—can be found in neon red lights, bookending each end of Kunath’s bar. A private space within the artist’s Los Angeles studio, the architecture and contents of the bar have been reproduced in the shared space of the gallery. title: Jordy Kerwick transforms everyday motifs into mythical fables in new show
summary: KÖNIG GALERIE present This Time Tomorrow by Australian-born, France-based artist Jordy Kerwick in the Vault of St. Agnes. Taking its title from The Kinks' 1970 song, the exhibition begins with a question: "This time tomorrow, where will we be?" The refrain captures a feeling of uncertainty about a future that seems near at hand yet remains indistinct. Across a group of recent oil and acrylic paintings, Kerwick turns the day-to-day into a site of meditation, where familiar motifs and fleeting impressions are transformed into vivid fables of the future. These works begin with small details: vivid greens, floral bursts of magenta, vermilion, and mauve, the presence of water, and the passing impressions of lived surroundings. title: Yossi Milo announces major museum acquisitions of works by Shikeith
summary: Yossi Milo announced that works by Shikeith have been acquired by the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Philadelphia, PA and The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, TX. This has been a year of great institutional interest in Shikeith, as the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust has recently unveiled Shikeith’s first public sculpture commission at Arts Landing in Pittsburgh, PA, while his work is currently on view at the Hammer Museum as part of their exhibition SPACE IS THE PLACE. The Philadelphia Museum of Art has acquired Phantasmatic Apparatus (2025) by Shikeith. Phantasmatic Apparatus draws on the visual language of seventeenth-century Dutch vanitas painting and the iconography of alchemy. This work situates Black spiritual practice within longer histories of ritual, belief, and invention. Scientific glassware, a vintage radio, and ceremonial

title: Lubaina Himid and Magda Stawarska reunite for immersive installation inspired by Zanzibar
summary: As part of the ongoing Lisson Street programme, the multidisciplinary artistic partnership of Lubaina Himid and Magda Stawarska present a new iteration of Zanzibar (1999-2023). Reflecting on themes of memory and movement, loss and belonging, this immersive and evocative mixed-media installation comprises nine diptychs painted by Himid in 1999, paired with a 38-minute multi-layered “libretto” composed by Stawarska in 2023. This historical series of canvases floats throughout the gallery – anchored by colourful cuboid forms and recurring zigzag patterns. It represents an anomalous passage of abstract painting and a decisive break from Himid's distinctly figurative, narrative-rich practice, being quite unlike “anything I made before or since,” as she has noted. title: Ayka Go shifts focus to nature and transformation in new series at Silverlens Manila
summary: Ayka Go undertakes a significant departure from the creased, folded and worn paper forms that have become emblematic of her practice, expanding her inquiry beyond the introspective terrain these motifs once occupied. For this new series, her attention shifts outward to the natural world, which becomes a framework through which processes of self-transformation are contemplated and understood. During a period of relative quietude in 2025, Ayka devoted considerable time to cultivating a garden at her studio. What began as an attempt to grow fruit-bearing trees and flowering plants gradually developed into a small ecosystem inhabited by butterflies, caterpillars, and dragonflies. title: Dynamic retrospective at Crocker Art Museum spans the highly original career of Suzanne Adan
summary: This summer, the Crocker Art Museum invites visitors to immerse themselves inside the personal universe of esteemed Sacramento artist Suzanne Adan. The artist’s first major retrospective—Suzanne Adan: I’m No Spring Chicken—combines fantasy, popular culture, and autobiography. Assembled in her 80th year, and titled by the artist, the exhibition showcases Adan’s sardonic wit, fondness for nostalgia, and spirit of mischievousness. Her technical mastery and range are featured in more than 100 examples of her playful paintings, drawings, prints, and ceramic sculptures. The exhibition is on view from June 28 through October 11, 2026. “Adan’s richly narrative paintings employ a personal and visual vocabulary that is most certainly American but informed by sources internationally,” says Scott A. title: Hyundai Artlab presents the 2026 Artlab Editorial Fellows
summary: Hyundai Artlab announced Travis Jeppesen and Yutong Lin as the recipients of the 2026 Artlab Editorial Fellowship. Now in its fourth year, the Artlab Editorial Fellowship extends Artlab Editorial’s mission to foster writing about today’s most compelling artists, celebrate connectivity in all its forms, and envision the future. This year’s Fellowship invites two art writers whose texts on contemporary art exercise critical empathy, navigating the balance between care and critique, the interrogative and intuitive, the perceptive and imaginative, and engage through dialogue to deepen understanding. Each Artlab Editorial Fellow will receive 10,000 dollars to produce three pieces of web-based writing for Artlab Editorial over the course of the year and will be paired with one of this year’s Fellowship Advisors, Mira Dayal and Gary Zhexi Zhang, for regular one-on-one guidance

title: Seattle Art Museum opens major exhibition on the Kondō ceramic dynasty
summary: The Seattle Art Museum opened The Kondō Family: Storytellers in Clay, a major exhibition bringing together 60 works by four artists across three generations. The show explores how each member of the Kondō family found new ways to innovate while navigating a storied tradition and serves as a retrospective of living artist Kondō Takahiro’s career. The exhibition runs from July 15, 2026, through January 3, 2027, at the Seattle Asian Art Museum. “The Kondō family’s work represents a century-long arc of technical mastery and persistent experimentation,” said Aaron Rio, SAM’s Tateuchi Foundation Curator of Japanese and Korean Art. “Each artist pays respect to tradition and family legacy by challenging it and pushing at its edges.” From wheel-thrown vases brushed with lively pictures of plants and landscapes to life-size self-portraits in porcelain,

title: Kate Newby covers Portland airport wall with 1,600 handbuilt ceramic tiles
summary: Laurel Gitlen congratulates to Kate Newby on her first permanent public commission, The Sound of Trees, now on view in the Arrivals Terminal of the Portland International Airport (PDX). The Sound of Trees is comprised of more than 1,600 handbuilt ceramic tiles and spans 75 feet. From a distance the work is an exhilarating abstract field of continuous colors and textures, while up close the richly textured surface holds the topographic impressions of pine needles, leaves, and puddled glass melted into the crags and depressions in the clay. Over several years, Newby developed this work collecting natural and found materials with students, artists and community members in Oregon and then used these elements in the making, glazing and firing of the tiles in her Texas studio.
